rationale: Claim 4 elaborates the control plane's operational role (trust granting, leased tokens) within the architectural split defined in Claim 1
Claim 5 elaborates the data plane side of the split by identifying three distinct PEP types
The control/data plane split is the architectural mechanism that enables lateral movement prevention by centralizing auth decisions
The PDP/PEP model provides the framework where the PDP (control plane) naturally functions as the trust grantor
Claim 5 extends the PDP/PEP model by identifying three concrete PEP types (user agent, network, application)
Temporary trust and leased tokens directly prevent lateral movement by requiring fresh authorization for each access
All three PEP types depend on the control plane (trust grantor) for authorization decisions
Multiple PEP types at different layers (network, app, user agent) close enforcement gaps that enable lateral movement
BSI explicitly derives its definition from the 'Assume Breach' approach, tracing lineage through Marsh, Jericho Forum, and Kindervag
BSI extends NIST's definition (including the positive tenets approach) with German regulatory emphasis on verifiable evidence (Nachweise)
Competing definitional frameworks: Claim 7 says ZT is defined by NIST's positive tenets; Claim 8 says ZT is defined through CISA's five-pillar model instead
Claim 7 defines ZT by what it positively DOES (seven tenets); Claim 10 defines ZT by the threat model (assume breach). These are opposing definitional approaches
NIST defines architecture first then threats (Ch 5); the NSA document does the opposite — opens with threat landscape before defining ZT. Claim 10 explicitly contrasts with NIST's approach
'Assume breach' provides the threat model that makes lateral movement prevention the primary architectural goal
The PDP/PEP model provides concrete enforcement architecture for NIST's technology-agnostic positive tenets
NIST's document structure (definitions → components → use cases) provides the organizing framework within which PDP/PEP is presented as a core component
The trust grantor model (temporary trust, leased tokens) is a concrete implementation supporting the positive tenets' technology-agnostic goals
Three PEP types provide layered enforcement supporting the positive tenets' mandate for continuous verification at every access point
